cards.name: Press release
cards.summary: A one-page announcement written the way a reporter would write the story: the news in the headline and first sentence, facts and numbers next, two quotes that carry opinion, then the 'About' boilerplate and a media contact. Good looks like a release a sub-editor can run with light edits; bad looks like an ad with a dateline.
use_for: Product or service launches with a date, price and place
Funding rounds, acquisitions, partnerships and senior hires
Milestones with a hard number (100th store, 1 lakh users, first export order)
Events, awards, reports and survey findings a reporter can quote
'Press notes' sent to Hindi and regional dailies for local business, NGO or institute news
avoid: No news, only a message: post it as a blog or genre:linkedin_post instead of spending a journalist's attention
A government department's announcement: use genre:government_press_note (PIB-style format and sign-off)
A tailored pitch to one reporter: write genre:media_pitch and attach the release
Bad news, a recall or an incident: use genre:crisis_statement or genre:apology_statement
Full company background, photos and fact sheets: those belong in genre:press_kit

cards.goal: A journalist decides from the headline and first paragraph that this is a story, then runs it or calls for an interview using your facts and quotes.

structure.does: 'For immediate release' or 'Embargoed until <date, time, IST>'. Use an embargo only when there is a real reason (results, an event start).
The news as a sentence with a strong verb: who did what, with the one number or place that makes it news. No adjectives the reporter would delete.
Adds the second most important fact (price, date, scale, who benefits).
CITY, Date: one or two sentences answering who, what, when, where and why it matters. A reader who stops here has the story.
The numbers and background that make it significant: market size you can source, before/after, how it works, availability and price.
Opinion, reason or ambition only a person can say; it must not repeat the facts. Name, title, company.
Specifics a reporter needs: dates, locations, eligibility, how to buy or apply, partner roles. Bullets are fine.
A partner, customer, investor or beneficiary adding an outside view.
'About <Company>': what it does, for whom, since when, scale, website. Same text on every release.
Name, phone, email (and WhatsApp if that is how Indian reporters will reach you); link to photos or press kit; '###' or '-ends-'.

length.note: Most releases fit one page. Regional-language press notes for local dailies run shorter (200-350 words); results or report releases run longer because of data tables.

checklist: Does the headline state the news with a verb, without 'announces' doing all the work?
Does the first sentence answer who, what and when, with the place in the dateline?
Could a reporter cut everything after paragraph two and still have an accurate story?
Does every quote carry an opinion or reason rather than repeating a fact?
Are claims like 'first', 'largest' or 'leading' either backed by a named source or removed?
Are dates, prices and numbers written as numerals with units (Rs, km, crore) and checked?
Is there an 'About' boilerplate and a named media contact with phone and email?
Is it free of internal jargon and acronyms a general reporter would not know?
Is it free of second-person sales language ('you', 'hurry', 'book now')?
pitfalls: Quote as filler ('We are delighted to announce this partnership'): reporters skip it. Make the quote say why it matters: 'Most Pune societies still have no charger within 5 km; we want that number at zero by 2027.'
News buried in paragraph three after company history: move the history to the boilerplate and lead with the event.
Unsupported superlatives ('India's first', 'revolutionary', 'world-class'): either cite who says so or state the fact that would make someone else say it.
Ad language and calls to buy: a release that reads like an ad gets binned or run as a paid advertorial. Keep 'you' and 'hurry' out; put buying details as plain facts.
One English release mailed to Hindi and Marathi dailies: transcreate the lead and quotes for each language desk and give a local spokesperson who can speak that language.
Huge attachments and no contact: link to a photo folder, name a person who answers the phone the day it goes out.
cards.exemplar_brief: Press release from a Pune EV-charging startup (ChargeKart, fictional) announcing 40 public fast chargers live across 25 housing societies in Baner, Wakad and Hinjewadi from 1 November, Rs 18 per kWh, booking via app; audience: business and city reporters at Pune and Mumbai dailies and EV trade sites; English; 350-450 words; one founder quote and one quote from a housing-society secretary; goal: reporters run the story or call for an interview.

verified.note: Runs as a story: 12-word verb headline, subhead adds price and booking, dateline lead covers who/what/when/where, both quotes carry opinion (why societies; secretary on opening bays to neighbours), key-details bullets, boilerplate, contact and ###. No superlatives, no 'you'. Context paragraph is thin on why it matters (no sourced market number, rightly not invented; a [placeholder: Pune EV figure, source] would have helped). Dateline 27 Oct 2026 is a Tuesday, 1 Nov a Sunday: fine.

cards.name: Pricing page copy
cards.summary: The words on a plans page: plan names, a who-it's-for line per plan, the price and its unit, the few features that separate tiers, a comparison table and a pricing FAQ. Good copy lets a buyer pick the right plan in under a minute without emailing sales; bad copy is a feature dump with the price hidden behind 'Contact us'.
use_for: SaaS plan pages with 2-4 tiers and a monthly/annual toggle
Service packages for agencies, studios and consultants (Starter / Growth / Retainer)
Course, cohort and membership tiers
D2C subscription plans (refill packs, meal plans, subscriptions with skip/cancel)
Pricing FAQ blocks and plan tooltips on an existing page
avoid: Selling the product from scratch to cold traffic: write genre:landing_page or genre:sales_page and link here
The checkout form, error and payment microcopy: use genre:order_form_checkout_copy
A side-by-side against named competitors: use genre:comparison_page
Pre-ticked add-ons, prices that grow at checkout, fake 'only 3 seats left' timers: these are dark patterns under the CCPA 2023 guidelines; show the full price and real limits instead

sources.title: Mighty Fine Copy: B2B SaaS copywriting rate card
sources.supports: fixed-price lines for brand messaging guide, landing page, full website copy

buyers: B2B SaaS founders and product marketers
Website copy agencies selling full-site packages
cards.value_why: Rarely bought alone: it is sold inside landing-page and full-website copy packages (Mighty Fine Copy's B2B SaaS rate card prices those as fixed lines). Worth doing well because it is the page with buying intent.
cards.goal: A visitor picks the plan that fits their situation and starts the trial, checkout or sales call without having to ask what is included.

structure.does: Says who the plans are for and the outcome, or answers the main worry ('Start free. Pay when you send your 51st invoice.'). Not 'Pricing'.
Monthly vs annual with the saving in rupees, currency, and whether GST is included or extra.

Each card: plan name that signals the buyer (Solo, Shop, Chain) rather than metal names; a who-it's-for line; price plus unit (per user / per month / per outlet); 3-6 lines saying what this tier adds; one CTA button with a verb.
structure.length: Per card: name 1-2 words, who-for 8-15 words, 3-6 feature lines of 3-8 words

structure.does: Marks one plan and says why in a few words ('Most shops with 2+ staff').
Grouped rows (Billing, Inventory, Support), plain feature names in the buyer's words, ticks or numbers, a short tooltip where a term needs it.
Logos, a count of customers with a date, or one testimonial that mentions price or value.
Answers the questions that block payment: free trial terms, GST invoice, upgrade/downgrade, cancel and refund, payment methods (UPI, cards, net banking), overage limits, data after cancelling.

structure.part: Custom / enterprise line and final CTA
structure.does: Who should talk to sales and what they get; repeat the main CTA.

length.note: Visible words on the page including table labels and FAQ. Simple products with one plan stay near the bottom; B2B tables with many rows and a long FAQ reach the top.

checklist: Does every plan have a who-it's-for line, not only a feature list?
Is every price shown with its unit (per month, per user, per outlet) and with GST stated as included or extra?
Can a reader tell in one line what each higher plan adds over the one below?
Is the same feature called by the same name on the cards, the table and the FAQ?
Does each CTA button use a verb that says what happens next (Start 14-day trial, Talk to sales)?
Does the FAQ answer cancel, refund, upgrade/downgrade and payment methods?
Are all limits and fees (overage, setup fee, add-ons) visible on this page rather than at checkout?
Is it free of fake scarcity or countdowns that are not tied to a real deadline?
pitfalls: Metal plan names (Silver, Gold, Platinum) that say nothing about the buyer: name plans by who they fit (Solo, Shop, Chain) or by size.
Twelve ticks per card: the buyer cannot see the difference. Put only the deltas on cards ('Everything in Shop, plus...') and the full list in the table.
Jargon feature names copied from the product backlog ('Multi-entity ledger sync'): use the buyer's words ('Run 2+ GST numbers from one login').
Price shown without GST or unit, then a bigger number at checkout: that is drip pricing under the CCPA dark-patterns guidelines. Show the full price or say '+18% GST' next to it.
Annual saving shown only as a percentage: rupees per year is easier to feel ('Save Rs 1,200 a year').
'Contact us' as the only price for small buyers: SMB buyers leave. Publish a starting price and keep 'Contact sales' for the custom tier.
cards.exemplar_brief: Pricing page copy for a Bengaluru GST-billing app for kirana and small retail shops (BillSaathi, fictional): three plans (Free up to 50 invoices a month; Shop Rs 399/month; Chain Rs 999/month for 3+ outlets), monthly/annual toggle with 2 months free on annual, a 12-row comparison table and 8 FAQs; English with one Hindi line per plan allowed; 350-500 words; goal: shop owners with 1-2 staff choose Shop and start the 14-day trial.

verified.note: Plans named by buyer (Free/Shop/Chain) with who-for lines, units, GST-inclusive note, rupee savings (Rs 798 / Rs 1,998, arithmetic checks), deltas only on cards, 12-row grouped table, 8 FAQs covering trial, switch, payment, GST invoice, cancel/refund and data. Natural Hinglish line per plan. One gap: an owner with exactly 2 outlets fits neither Shop (1) nor Chain (3+); say which plan they take. 'Customer udhar ledger' is a Shop delta missing from the Shop card.

cards.name: Print ad copy (newspaper / magazine)
cards.summary: Headline, visual idea, body copy and response block for a newspaper or magazine ad that has to win attention on a page full of news. Good print copy has one idea that the headline and picture deliver together, body copy that keeps the promise with specifics, and response details a reader can act on without a link.
use_for: Newspaper ads for retail launches, festive offers, real-estate projects, admissions and hospitals
Magazine ads for premium and lifestyle brands
Regional-language press ads transcreated from an English master
Recruitment, tender-style and public-notice style display ads that still need to persuade
Long-copy brand ads where the reader has time (Sunday supplements, trade magazines)
avoid: Roadside hoardings and transit: use genre:ooh_billboard_copy (5-7 words, read in seconds)
Paid content made to look like an article: use genre:advertorial and follow its labelling rules
Leaflets, mailers and brochures where the reader holds the piece: genre:brochure_copy or genre:direct_mail_package
Digital banners: genre:display_banner_ad_copy (clickable, tiny, animated)

cards.goal: A reader flipping the page stops on the ad, gets the one idea from headline and picture, and calls, visits, scans or remembers the brand at the moment of choice.

structure.does: Carries the whole idea or the news on its own: the benefit, the offer or a provocation the picture resolves. Written for the reader who reads nothing else.
One line telling the art director what the picture shows and how it works with the headline. Headline and picture should add up to one thought, not repeat each other.
Bridges headline to body with the main fact: price, date, place.
First sentence picks up the headline's promise; then reasons and specifics (numbers, names, proof); short paragraphs. Long copy only where the reader has time and the product needs explaining.
structure.length: 0-60 words for small or offer ads; 80-250 for brand or explanation ads

structure.does: Exactly what to do: price, offer dates, address with landmark, phone/WhatsApp number, QR code with what it opens, website typed out.
Legal and regulatory lines the category requires (T&C, RERA registration and website for property, disclaimers, statutory warnings). Get the exact text from the client.
Logo plus tagline or brand line.

length.note: Ad size decides it: a strip or quarter-page offer ad lives on headline + 30-60 words; a full-page brand or long-copy ad can carry 200-300. Count the response block and mandatories.

checklist: Does the headline work on its own for a reader who reads nothing else?
Do the headline and the visual note make one idea together, without saying the same thing twice?
Does the body's first sentence follow straight from the headline?
Is every claim specific and supportable (number, name, date) rather than an adjective?
Does the response block give a phone/WhatsApp number, address or typed-out URL a reader can use without a link?
Are offer dates and conditions stated, with T&C pointing to where the full terms are?
Are the category's mandatories present (or flagged for the client to supply)?
Is there exactly one main message, not three competing offers?
For a regional-language version: is it transcreated (idiom, wordplay) rather than translated word for word?
pitfalls: Label headline ('Grand Opening Sale', 'Admissions Open'): every ad on the page says it. State what is different: 'Full-body check-up at home, Rs 999, report on WhatsApp in 24 hours'.
Digital CTAs in print ('click here', 'link in bio', 'swipe up'): print readers cannot click. Give a typed URL, a QR code and say what it opens, or a number.
Picture and headline saying the same thing (photo of a car, headline 'The new car'): let the headline add what the picture cannot show.
Copy written in English and translated literally into Hindi or Tamil: puns die and register goes stiff. Brief a native writer to transcreate from the idea, not the words.

Coaching or education ads promising ranks, '100% selection' or showing toppers without consent and facts: the CCPA 2024 coaching guidelines target exactly this. State verifiable results with the course and year.
Mandatories forgotten until the press deadline: list the required lines in the first draft and leave space for them.

require.label: has a response detail (number, address, URL or visit/call verb)

ban.label: digital-only CTA in print
ban.regex: (?i)\b(click here|click (the|this) link|swipe up|link in bio|tap (the|this) link)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Quarter-page ad in a Hindi daily's Patna edition for a Patna diagnostics lab (Sehat Diagnostics, fictional) launching free home sample collection across Patna city with a Rs 999 full-body check-up package (62 tests) and reports on WhatsApp within 24 hours; audience: families with parents over 50; Hindi (Devanagari); headline + visual note + 50-90 words of body + response block with phone/WhatsApp number and address; goal: readers call or WhatsApp to book a home collection.

verified.note: Headline carries the idea alone (maa-babuji test at home, Rs 999); visual note adds 'no lab, no queue' instead of repeating it; subhead gives 62 tests, free collection, 24-h WhatsApp report; body 73 words of natural Hindi; response block and mandatories flagged for the client; no NABL claim invented. Craft slip: the headline and opening address the grown-up children, but the last body line ('report you can send to the children living away') addresses the parents; pick one reader.

cards.name: Product description (D2C / ecommerce)
cards.summary: The copy on a product page: title, an opening line on who it is for and what it does for them, benefit-led bullets, specs, how to use, and the answers that remove the last doubt (size, returns, delivery). Good copy reads like a knowledgeable shop assistant who has used the product; bad copy is adjectives ('premium quality', 'best-in-class') a buyer cannot check.
use_for: Product pages on a D2C Shopify or WooCommerce store
Marketplace listings (Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa, Meesho, Etsy) within each platform's fields and limits
Bulk SKU descriptions from a spec sheet, written to one template
Rewriting supplier copy so it matches the brand voice and is not duplicated across sellers
Product data feeds for Google Shopping and AI shopping agents
avoid: The rich image modules below an Amazon listing: genre:amazon_a_plus_content
A collection or category page: genre:category_page
A long sales letter for a high-ticket single product: genre:sales_page
Packaging panels and labels: genre:packaging_copy (space and legal lines differ)
Health, cure or 'clinically proven' claims without the brand's evidence on file: write the observable benefit instead

Often bought in bulk (dozens to hundreds of SKUs), so speed with consistency is the skill being paid for.
cards.goal: A shopper who landed on the page understands what the product does for them, has their last doubt answered, and adds it to cart.

structure.does: Brand + product type + the attribute people search and filter by (size, material, variant, count). Follow the marketplace's title rules; no promo words in the title.
structure.length: 6-15 words (check the platform card for its limit)

structure.does: Who it is for and the main result, in the buyer's words. Answers 'why this one?'
Each bullet starts with the benefit, then the feature that proves it (feature to benefit). Order by what buyers ask about most (use reviews and support tickets).
Material, dimensions, weight, ingredients, compatibility, size chart link, care instructions, country of origin. Facts from the spec sheet only.
Steps or dosage-free usage tips; what to expect and when.

structure.part: What's in the box / pack size
structure.does: Exactly what arrives.
Returns, warranty, delivery time, COD availability, as the store actually offers them.
Answers the 2-4 questions that come up in reviews or chats (fit, taste, shelf life, works with X?).

structure.part: SEO title and meta description (own store only)
structure.does: Search-facing versions of the title and opening line.

length.note: Low-price impulse items (socks, a snack pack) need 50-100 words; considered purchases (mattress, mixer-grinder, skincare actives) need 200-350 plus specs and FAQ. Marketplaces cap fields; obey the platform card over this range.

checklist: Does the opening line say who the product is for and what it does for them?
Does every bullet lead with a benefit and back it with a feature or fact?
Are size, material or ingredients, quantity and compatibility stated from the spec sheet?
Is every claim checkable (a number, a test, a material) rather than an adjective like 'premium'?
Does it answer the most common pre-purchase question for this category (fit, taste, shelf life, warranty)?
Are returns, delivery and COD stated the way the store actually offers them?
Does the title follow the target platform's format without promo words or ALL CAPS?
Is it free of health, cure or safety claims the brand cannot substantiate?
Does it read in the brand's voice and differ from the supplier's copy used by other sellers?
pitfalls: Adjective soup ('premium quality, best-in-class, top-notch'): replace each with the fact behind it: '180 GSM combed cotton', '3-layer stitched hem'.
Features with no 'so what' ('BPA-free Tritan'): add the benefit: 'BPA-free Tritan, so it does not hold the smell of yesterday's nimbu paani'.
Copy pasted from the manufacturer: every seller has the same text and the page competes with itself. Rewrite from reviews and the brand voice.

Health or cure claims on food, supplements and cosmetics ('cures hair fall', 'no side effects'): misleading-ad rules apply. Describe what the product contains and how people use it; leave efficacy to approved claims.
Same template for every SKU with only the colour swapped: buyers and search engines see thin pages. Add the variant's real difference (use-case, fit note, pairing).
Mandatory declarations (MRP, net quantity, manufacturer, origin) invented or guessed: take them from the label data and flag gaps to the client.
cards.exemplar_brief: Shopify product page for a Pune D2C brand's 1-litre wood-pressed groundnut oil (Ghanibaba, fictional; pressed in a wooden ghani at low speed, unrefined, glass bottle, best before 6 months); audience: urban home cooks aged 28-45 moving away from refined oil; English with one Marathi or Hindi word allowed; title + 30-word opening + 5 bullets + specs + 3 FAQs + SEO title and meta description, 150-250 words in all; goal: add to cart.

verified.note: Title in Shopify format, 30-word opening with 'so your tadka smells of groundnuts', benefit-first bullets, specs with MRP/FSSAI/policy placeholders, no health or smoke-point claims; 'unrefined = no bleaching or deodorising' is correct. Weak spots: 'best before 6 months' appears three times and two of three FAQs restate bullets; the questions buyers of kachi ghani oil actually ask (sediment or cloudiness, storage, deep frying) are not answered. Fifth bullet ('a date to plan around') is not a benefit.

cards.name: Product review article
cards.summary: A hands-on review of one product or service: what was tested, how, for how long, what the numbers showed, what was good and bad, how it compares with the obvious alternatives, and a clear verdict on who should buy it. Good reviews carry first-hand evidence a reader cannot get from the spec sheet; bad ones rewrite the spec sheet and end with 'overall a great product'.
use_for: Tech, appliance, gadget and software reviews on blogs and publisher sites
Service reviews (a bank account, a course, a coworking space, a travel card)
Affiliate content where the buyer decision is one product, yes or no
Long-term or 'after 6 months' reviews that update an earlier first look
Video review scripts that need a written companion article
avoid: Several products ranked: genre:best_of_roundup or genre:comparison_article
Reviews written mainly to earn commissions across a niche: genre:affiliate_review covers that business model and its disclosures
Films, books, restaurants and art judged as works: genre:critical_review
A product you have not used or tested: write a spec explainer and say so, or do not write it

cards.goal: A reader deciding whether to buy this product finishes knowing whether it suits their use, what they give up, and what to buy instead if it does not.

structure.does: Product name + 'review' + the angle or test (duration, use-case): 'Mi Air Purifier 4 review: 30 days in a Delhi November'.
One- or two-sentence verdict, buy if / skip if, price paid and date checked, score only if the site uses one.
How the product was obtained (bought, loaned, free from brand) and whether links earn a commission. Before the first link.
Duration, setting, conditions, tools and what was measured; who the tester is in relation to the product.
One section per decision factor (build, performance, battery, noise, app, cost of running). Each: what you expected, what you measured, what it means for the reader. Numbers, photos with captions.
Specific, earned by the tests above, not generic ('loud on turbo: 58 dB at 1 m').
2-3 named rivals and when each is the better pick.

structure.part: Who should buy / who should skip
structure.does: Map the verdict to reader situations (room size, budget, use).

structure.part: Final verdict and where to buy
structure.does: Restate the call; links to more than one seller where possible; date of price check.
What changed since publication (firmware, price, long-term issues).

length.note: Cheap, simple products need 1,000-1,500; complex or expensive ones (laptops, cars, financial products) with many decision factors reach 2,500-3,000. Length should come from tests, not padding.

checklist: Is there a verdict with 'buy if' and 'skip if' in the first screen?
Does the article say how long and under what conditions the product was tested?
Does it include at least three measured or observed numbers from the reviewer's own testing?
Are there real cons, each tied to a test or observation?
Does it name 2-3 alternatives and say when each is the better choice?
Is the disclosure (free product, affiliate links) placed before the first buying link?
Is any 'best' claim backed by the comparison that earned it?
Are price and availability dated?
Could a reader tell this was written by someone who used the product (photos, quirks, specifics no spec sheet has)?
pitfalls: Spec-sheet rewrite with no testing: Google's review guidance asks for first-hand evidence and measurements. If you cannot test, say what you checked and how, or turn it into a spec explainer.
Pros only, cons like 'a bit pricey': readers stop trusting the verdict. Find the real trade-off ('filter costs Rs 2,400 every 6 months').
Disclosure in the footer: ASCI and FTC rules want it where the reader sees it before the link. Put one line under the verdict box.
Verdict that hedges ('it depends on your needs'): say whose needs. 'Buy it for a 1BHK; skip it for a hall bigger than 400 sq ft.'
Prices quoted without a date: they go stale in weeks. Write 'Rs 9,999 on 3 Oct 2026' and keep the update log.
Copying star ratings or reviews from marketplaces as if they were your own: cite them as other buyers' ratings, never as your test.
cards.exemplar_brief: Hands-on review of a Rs 9,000-12,000 HEPA air purifier used for 30 days in a 2BHK in Dwarka, Delhi in November, for a Delhi home-appliance review blog with affiliate links to two sellers; editor's test notes below; English; 1,500-2,000 words; goal: the reader decides buy or skip and knows which alternative fits a bigger room. Editor's notes (demo data for this test; brand and model invented): Airvana Home 300, bought with the blog's own money for Rs 10,499 on Saturday 1 November 2025; tested 1-30 November in a 132 sq ft bedroom, door shut, auto mode, about 16 hours a day; the maker rates it for up to 330 sq ft. Handheld PM2.5 monitor averages (ug/m3): outdoors 268 in the morning and 341 at night; bedroom 38 in the morning and 55 at night. Noise at 1 m: sleep mode 28 dB, low 36, medium 47, high 58. Replacement filter Rs 2,400, rated 6 months; the indicator showed 22% used after 30 days. App issues: lost Wi-Fi after every router restart (re-paired 3 times); schedules reset after the firmware update on day 19. Prices checked Monday 1 December 2025 (the two affiliate links): Rs 10,299 on Amazon.in, Rs 10,999 on the maker's store. Why this person, why now: the bigger trend, stake or tension the profile explains, with one fact that proves it is real.
How they got here, in a few decisive beats (a choice, a failure, a turn), not a CV.
Two to four scenes from observation, with quotes from the subject and from 2-4 other people (colleague, customer, family, rival, official). Each quote adds something the writer cannot say.
The doubt, criticism, risk or unsolved problem, with the critic's voice and the subject's answer.
A kicker: a scene or quote that lands the theme or opens the next question. No summary.

CV opening ('Born in 1985 in Gaya, she studied...'): open on a scene and move biography to the middle.

Praise adjectives ('an inspiring trailblazer'): show the act that would make a reader think it.

structure.does: List the fields each row needs; mark which are required for a page to exist; define the noindex or no-page rule for rows with thin data (e.g. fewer than N real data points, no reviews, no price).

structure.part: Title tag, H1 and meta pattern

Two or three sentences answering the query using row data (price band, transit time, what syncs), not a generic welcome.

Questions answered from the row's data; never the same five FAQs on every page.
To the parent hub, nearby or related rows, and the main product page, with descriptive anchor text.

Is there a noindex or no-page rule for rows with thin data?
Does the intro answer the query with row data, not generic text?
Would two neighbouring pages (e.g. two cities) differ in more than the swapped keyword?
Do the title and H1 patterns read naturally for the longest and shortest values, with fallbacks for missing ones?
Are there conditional blocks that change the copy based on the data?
Are FAQs generated from row data rather than identical on every page?
Do internal links point to the hub and related rows with descriptive anchors?
Is there one CTA that matches the page's query?

Thin rows published anyway: set a data threshold and noindex or merge rows that fail it.
AI-written paragraphs per row with no new facts: same problem, more words. Facts come from the data; prose only explains them.
Same FAQ block everywhere: it adds duplicate text and no value. Generate questions from what differs per row.
No hub page: hundreds of orphan pages. Plan the hub, the internal links and the crawl path with the template.

Fake countdowns and 'last chance' sent four times: CCPA's dark-patterns guidelines name false urgency; readers learn to ignore you. Set a real deadline and keep it.
Offer only inside a banner image: many inboxes block images and screen readers skip it. Put the offer in live text and alt text.
Five buttons and a full catalogue grid: attention splits. One button, two to four picks.
Terms hidden ('*T&C apply' with no terms): state the main condition next to the offer and link the rest.
Mailing people who never opted in or cannot unsubscribe: deliverability and consent problems (CAN-SPAM, GDPR, DPDP). Mail only your consented list and honour unsubscribes fast.

ban.label: spam-trigger phrasing
ban.regex: (?i)\b(act now|click here|once in a lifetime|you have been selected|100% free|winner)\b

ban.label: all-caps shouting (3+ caps words in a row)

cards.exemplar_brief: Diwali sale email from a Jaipur hand-block-print home linen D2C brand (Neel Ghar, fictional) to its 18,000-subscriber list: 25% off bedsheet sets and 15% off table linen, Thursday to Sunday 11:59 pm IST, free shipping above Rs 1,499, code not needed; English body with one Hinglish subject-line variant; subject + preheader + 120-180 words + one button; goal: subscribers click through to the Diwali collection and buy before Sunday midnight.

verified.note: Subject names offer and deadline, Hinglish variant reads naturally, preheader adds table linen, free shipping and no code; real reason for the offer (Diwali guests, new sheets), offer lines with exclusions, end day and time in IST, one button, P.S. restating the deadline, footer with unsubscribe and sender. Weekday-only dates follow the brief. The 'choose the colours... nothing to remember at payment' paragraph repeats 'no code needed' and could go.

cards.name: Public service announcement (PSA)
cards.summary: A short non-commercial message (audio or video script, poster, WhatsApp card or mic announcement) that asks citizens to adopt one safe or civic behaviour. Good PSAs name one behaviour, give one reason the audience cares about and one doable action with the where and when, in the language people speak at home; bad PSAs list six instructions in official Hindi and scare without telling anyone what to do.
use_for: Health behaviours: vaccination days, dengue source reduction, ORS and zinc, TB treatment completion
Road safety, fire safety and disaster preparedness messages
Voter awareness and enrolment drives
Cyber-fraud awareness (OTP sharing, fake KYC calls) with the reporting route
Scheme enrolment and camp announcements by district administrations and NGOs
CSR awareness campaigns on water, sanitation and girls' education
avoid: Selling a product or service: genre:radio_spot_script, genre:tvc_script or genre:video_ad_script
Explaining a scheme's full eligibility and documents: genre:scheme_explainer
A department's formal news release: genre:government_press_note
Party or candidate messaging: genre:political_social_commentary or genre:political_speech, under election rules
Fear appeals with no doable action: give the action and where to do it, or do not run the scare

sources.title: MyGov
sources.supports: government citizen-engagement platform that runs awareness campaigns

buyers: Police cyber cells and traffic police
NGOs, CSR foundations and UN agencies
cards.value_why: Government departments, NGOs and CSR foundations commission awareness campaigns from IEC (information, education, communication) budgets; MyGov runs citizen awareness campaigns. Usually bought as part of a campaign with design and media, not per script.
cards.goal: A listener or viewer does one specific safe or civic action (this Sunday, at this place, by calling this number) and tells someone at home.

structure.does: A situation the audience recognises from their own day, or a short question; for audio, a sound that belongs to their life.
One fact that makes the behaviour matter, in everyday words, from a named authority's data or advice.
One action, concrete and doable: who does what, when, with what.
The helpline, camp location, timing, or the 2-3 steps. Repeat the number in audio.
What the family or community gains, framed positively (safe children, a saved day's wages).
Issuing authority or NGO, helpline, campaign line; logo for visuals.

length.note: Posters and WhatsApp cards: 15-40 words. 30-second audio/video: about 55-75 spoken words. 60-second mic or radio announcements in villages: up to 150. Fewer words for lower-literacy and older audiences.

checklist: Does the piece ask for exactly one behaviour?
Is the action doable by the audience this week, with the place, time or number given?
Is the risk stated as one fact from a named authority, not an invented statistic?
Are words everyday spoken language for this region, with no official or medical jargon?
If there is fear or risk, is it paired with the action that removes it?
Is it free of blame or shame aimed at the people it wants to change?
Does the sign-off name the issuing authority or NGO and the helpline?
For audio: is the number or place repeated and said slowly?
If AI-generated voices, faces or scenes are used, is the synthetic-content label planned?
pitfalls: Six messages in one spot (mosquito nets, coolers, fever, hospital, cleanliness, helpline): nothing sticks. Pick the one behaviour this campaign phase needs.
Official Hindi ('vector-janit rogon ki rokthaam hetu'): people tune out. Say 'machhar ka anda paani mein palta hai'.
Fear without a door ('Dengue can kill your child'): fear with no doable action makes people look away. Follow the risk with the 10-minute Sunday task.
Blaming the audience ('Lazy people let water collect'): blame triggers defence. Speak to the caring parent instead.
Statistics nobody can source: use the health department's or WHO's figure with the source, or skip the number.
Election-period messaging that features ministers or party symbols: under the Model Code of Conduct, check with the election office before release.
cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second audio PSA for a Patna municipal health office, played on local FM and as a WhatsApp voice note: every Sunday, spend 10 minutes emptying and scrubbing coolers, flower pots, tyres and water drums so dengue mosquitoes cannot breed; audience: households in Patna's dense mohallas; Hindi with Bhojpuri flavour; 55-75 spoken words with one sound cue; sign-off with the municipal health helpline (number supplied by the client as [HELPLINE]); goal: households do the Sunday 10-minute check.

verified.note: One behaviour (Sunday 10-minute empty, scrub, dry, refill of coolers, pots, tyres, drums), one correct fact (the dengue mosquito breeds in clean standing water), benefit framed positively, helpline repeated slowly, a sound cue from the listener's own summer (cooler hum and drip), no blame or fear. Bhojpuri-flavoured verbs (dekhni, dela, rahi, bata din) sound natural; 'surakshit' is bookish, 'bachal rahi' would fit better. Time it aloud: 63 words plus two ten-digit readings may run past 30 seconds.

cards.name: Push notification / in-app message copy
cards.summary: Title and body (plus button labels and deep link) for app or web push and in-app messages that bring a user back to do one thing. Good push copy fits before the OS truncates it, names something specific to this user, and lands on the exact screen it promises; bad push is 'Hey there! We miss you' sent daily until the user switches notifications off.
use_for: Re-engagement pushes for inactive users
Transactional and status pushes (order shipped, payment due, class starts in 15 minutes)
Cart, wishlist and price-drop reminders
Onboarding sequences that teach one feature per message
In-app modals, banners and tooltips announcing a feature or offer
Web push for publishers and ecommerce sites
avoid: Long explanations or several offers at once: send an email (genre:promotional_email) and keep the push to the hook
Buttons, errors and empty states inside the product: genre:ux_microcopy
Text messages: genre:sms_marketing (DLT templates in India)
WhatsApp campaigns: genre:whatsapp_broadcast
Scare copy ('Your account will be blocked') that is not true: it trains users to ignore you and mirrors phishing

sources.title: CleverTap: Mobile copywriting tips for push notifications & in-app messages (updated 2025-10-25)
sources.supports: Suggests keeping push and in-app copy short (it cites roughly 20-90 characters for visibility), leading with value, personalising with context, using action verbs, one message per in-app screen, and testing send times; case notes: ZEE5 reported a 60% CTR increase from personalised timing plus copy testing; Dream11 found afternoon messages before events drove the highest engagement

sources.title: CleverTap: Welcome push notifications
sources.supports: onboarding push sequences as a CRM deliverable

sources.title: Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 (2026-02-04)
sources.supports: top-10 most in-demand Sales & Marketing skills include 'Marketing Automation'

buyers: Consumer app CRM and growth teams
cards.value_why: CleverTap (an Indian-founded engagement platform) publishes mobile-copy and onboarding-push playbooks with Indian app case notes (ZEE5, Dream11); Marketing Automation is in Upwork's top-10 marketing skills for 2026. Mostly written by in-house CRM teams, so freelance work comes as campaign sets and A/B variant packs.
cards.goal: The user taps the notification and completes the one action it promised on the screen it opens.

structure.does: Who gets it and why now (segment, event, time). Copy is written for that moment, not for 'all users'.
The hook in the first words: the specific thing for this user (their item, their streak, their class time). Check the platform card for where it truncates.
The detail that earns the tap and the action, in one or two short lines. One idea.
Every token ({{first_name}}, {{item}}, {{city}}) has a fallback that still reads naturally if empty.
Verb-first labels for the 1-2 actions.
The exact screen the copy promises (the cart, the class, the half-done lesson), not the home screen.
Headline, 1-2 lines of body, one primary button and a dismiss that does not guilt-trip.

length.note: Title plus body per message. Lock-screen space is small and varies by OS and device (see plat:push_notification_apns and plat:push_notification_fcm); front-load so the truncated version still works. Deliver 2-3 variants per message for testing.

checklist: Does the title make sense on its own if the body is cut off?
Does the message refer to something specific to this user or moment?
Is there one action, and does the deep link open the screen for it?
Does every personalisation token have a fallback that reads naturally?
Is any urgency real (an actual deadline, low stock, a class time)?
Is it free of guilt or scare tactics and of false account warnings?
Is the language the one this user chose in the app?
Are 2-3 variants supplied for testing?
For lending, gaming or finance apps: does it avoid promotions that sector rules restrict?
pitfalls: Generic 'We miss you!' blasts: specific beats cute. 'Your 12-day streak ends tonight. 1 workout, 7 minutes.'
Token without fallback ('Hi {{first_name}}' rendering as 'Hi ,'): set fallbacks ('Hi there' or drop the greeting) and test with empty data.
Deep link to the home screen: the user hunts for the promised thing and leaves. Link to the cart, the lesson, the order.
Daily nagging with the same message: CCPA's 2023 dark-patterns guidelines list nagging; users also turn notifications off. Cap frequency and vary the reason.
Fake urgency ('Last chance!' every week) and fake alerts ('Your account will be blocked'): erodes trust and looks like fraud. Use real deadlines only.
Pushing money-game offers or loan pitches without checking the 2025 online-gaming law and RBI digital-lending directions: some of this promotion is now restricted. Check before writing.

A set file is linted as one text: the word, exclamation and emoji caps count across all its messages. Check each message against its own length (5-35 words, title plus body) and lint each message from its own file before sending.

ban.label: scare copy that mimics fraud alerts

cards.exemplar_brief: Re-engagement set for a Pune fitness app (FitGully, fictional) for users inactive 7 days who had a streak before: three push variants (title + body + deep link to 'Today's 7-minute workout' + fallback for {{first_name}} and {{last_streak}}) and one in-app message shown on their return; Hinglish in Roman script plus one English variant; each push 8-25 words; goal: the user opens the app and logs one workout today.

verified.note: Trigger note, three variants with titles that work alone, real tokens with natural fallbacks, deep link to the workout screen not home, verb buttons, in-app message with a non-guilt dismiss, no fake urgency. Hinglish slip: Variant A 'Pichli baar {{last_streak}} din lagatar chale the' assumes a male user; use a gender-neutral line such as 'Pichli streak {{last_streak}} din ki thi'. lint_suspect upheld: max_words 45 is per message, the set fails as one file. CARD FIX: lint.max_words -> 300 for a full set file, or state in the card that each message is linted from its own file. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_c): lint.max_words 45 -> 300 for a full set file, plus a pitfall to lint each message from its own file; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Query letter (to literary agents)
cards.summary: A one-page letter that pitches a finished manuscript to a literary agent or editor so they ask to read pages. It gives the housekeeping (title, genre, word count), a story description that reads like strong back-cover copy, two comparable titles and a short bio. Good queries make the agent curious about one character's choice; bad ones open with a rhetorical question and explain the book's themes.
use_for: Querying US and UK literary agents for fiction and narrative non-fiction
Submitting to Indian publishers and agents who ask for a cover letter with sample chapters
Pitching small presses and editors who accept unagented submissions
Query critique and rewrite services for authors
avoid: Non-fiction sold on proposal: write genre:book_proposal (the query then points to it)
Back-cover or Amazon copy for a published book: genre:book_blurb or genre:kdp_book_description
A full plot summary including the ending: genre:synopsis (sent only if the agent asks)
Querying an unfinished novel: finish and revise first; fiction is pitched complete

sources.title: Jane Friedman: How to Write a Query Letter That Gets Manuscript Requests
sources.supports: query anatomy: housekeeping, story description (150-300 words), comps, bio (50-100 words); whole query about 200 to 450 words

cards.value_why: Reedsy sells query-letter review as an editorial service; demand sits mostly in US/UK trade publishing and each author needs one letter, so it is a small, occasional job, usually bundled with a synopsis or manuscript critique.
cards.goal: The agent requests the first pages or the full manuscript.

structure.does: One sentence on why this agent, only if it is real (a book they represent, something they asked for publicly). Otherwise skip it.
Title, genre/category, complete word count, and optionally the comps; can sit at the start or the end.
Protagonist and what they want, the inciting problem, what stands in the way, the stakes, and the choice they face. Present tense, specific details, voice of the book. Do not reveal the ending.
Two recent books that share audience or feel (not blockbusters), each with a phrase on what is similar.
Relevant credentials: publications, prizes, expertise or lived experience that matters to this book. Skip 'I have always loved writing'.
Thank the agent; note what is attached per their guidelines; contact details.

length.note: One page (Jane Friedman's range is about 200-450 words). Genre and the agent's guidelines decide the extras (pages pasted below the query are not counted).

checklist: Does it state title, genre and an exact, rounded word count?
Does the description name the protagonist, what they want, what blocks them and what they stand to lose?
Does the description end on the choice or stakes rather than revealing the ending?
Are there two comparable titles that are recent and not mega-bestsellers?
Is the bio limited to credentials relevant to this book?
Is the whole letter under one page (about 450 words or fewer)?
Is it addressed to a named agent, with any personalisation true?
Is it free of rhetorical-question openings, themes-talk and praise of the book by the author?
pitfalls: Rhetorical-question or 'Imagine a world' openings: agents read many a day. Open with the character and the situation.
Themes instead of plot ('a story about love, loss and identity'): show the events that carry the theme.
Too many names and subplots: keep the protagonist, the antagonist or main obstacle, and one ally.
Blockbuster comps ('the next Harry Potter'): signals no market awareness. Use recent books in your shelf space.
Word count far outside the category norm, or not stated: state it; if it is very long, cut the book before querying.
Mass 'Dear Agent' emails and ignored guidelines (attachments when they want pasted pages): follow each agent's instructions exactly.

ban.label: query cliches
ban.regex: (?i)\b(imagine a world|have you ever wondered|the next (harry potter|bestseller)|my (mom|mother|friends|family) (loved|love) it)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Query letter to a named London literary agent who represents upmarket fiction, for an 88,000-word debut upmarket novel set in Patna: a coaching-centre physics teacher discovers that his younger brother runs the exam paper-leak racket his students depend on, and must choose between his brother and the students he promised to get into IIT; author bio supplied (Patna-born, 10 years teaching in Kota and Patna, short stories in two Indian literary magazines); comps supplied by the author as [COMP 1] and [COMP 2]; English; 300-400 words; goal: the agent requests the first 50 pages.

verified.note: Housekeeping in one line, present-tense description with protagonist, want, inciting discovery, the bind (turn in his brother or keep teaching on a lie) and stakes, no ending revealed, comps and magazine names left to the author, bio limited to relevant lived experience, guideline-aware close. For a London agent, gloss Kota and IIT in a few words; the third paragraph is slightly abstract where one concrete scene beat (the exam date, a named student) would sharpen it.

cards.name: Quora answer
cards.summary: An expert answer to a Quora question that solves it in the first lines, backs it with first-hand experience and specifics, and links out only where it genuinely helps. Good answers read like advice from someone who has done it; bad answers are blog intros with a 'check out my course' link.
use_for: Exam, career, study-abroad and tech questions where Indian readers still search Quora
Building an expert's credibility in a narrow niche (CA, UPSC, coding, fitness)
Answering questions about your own field without selling
Quora Spaces posts for a niche community
Turning recurring client questions into reusable public answers
avoid: Subreddit posts and community threads: genre:reddit_post (different norms and audience)
FAQ content on your own site: genre:faq_answer_article
Replies under your own social posts: genre:comment_reply
Disguised ads or answers to questions you planted: readers and moderators spot them; write a disclosed answer or none

sources.title: Fiverr: Social Media Copywriting category (Platform facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Fiverr's Platform filter with live gig counts, a SUPPLY signal: Instagram 1910, Facebook 1663, LinkedIn 1338, TikTok 1009, Pinterest 376, Threads 238, Snapchat 123, Reddit 96, Twitter 47, Discord 5, Quora 3

buyers: Agencies running community and forum programmes
cards.value_why: Fiverr's social copy category listed Quora at only 3 gigs on 2026-10-04 (against 1,910 for Instagram), so it is rarely commissioned on its own; it survives as part of authority-building retainers for experts whose audience still reads Quora.
cards.goal: The asker gets a usable answer in the first lines, and readers upvote, follow the writer or open the one link because it adds depth.

structure.does: Why you can answer, in one line or via the answer credential ('Cleared SSC CGL 2019 while working at a bank').
The answer to the question as asked, complete enough that a reader who stops here is helped.
How you know: steps, numbers, what you or your clients did, what happened. Short paragraphs or a list.
One concrete case that shows the advice working or failing.
When the answer changes (different stream, state, budget, level).
One link that adds depth, with what it contains and your affiliation if it is yours.

length.note: Factual one-fact questions need 80-150 words; 'how should I prepare' or career questions earn 300-800 with steps. Length should come from usable specifics.

checklist: Do the first three sentences answer the question as asked?
Is there a line saying why the writer can answer?
Does the answer include specifics from first-hand experience (numbers, timelines, names of resources)?
Are caveats given for readers whose situation differs?
Is there at most one link, and does it add depth rather than repeat the answer?
If the link or product is the writer's own, is that disclosed?
Is it free of hashtags, 'DM me' and 'check out my course' lines?
For finance, health or legal questions: does it avoid personalised advice the writer is not registered to give?
pitfalls: Throat-clearing intro ('This is a very good question that many people ask...'): answer in line one.
Generic listicle copied from a blog: readers want what you did. Add your timetable, scores, mistakes.
Answer as an ad ('Join my batch, DM for fees'): collapsed or downvoted, and it burns the profile. Give the full answer; one disclosed link at the end at most.
Stock tips or 'guaranteed returns' advice from an unregistered writer: SEBI's finfluencer restrictions make this risky for anyone associated. Explain concepts, not calls.
Coaching institutes posting topper claims and rank promises: the CCPA 2024 coaching guidelines apply to these claims too.
One answer pasted under twenty similar questions: rewrite for each question's exact ask or link to your best answer.

ban.label: throat-clearing or chatbot opener
ban.regex: (?i)\b(great question|very good question|thanks for the a2a|this is a common question)\b

ban.label: hard sell lines
ban.regex: (?i)\b(dm me|check out my (course|channel|website|page)|link in (bio|profile)|join my batch)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Quora answer to 'How should a working professional prepare for SSC CGL in 6 months?' written as a Lucknow SSC mentor (persona notes supplied: cleared CGL in 2019 while working full-time at a bank branch, studied 2.5 hours on weekdays and 6 on Sundays, now mentors about 40 aspirants a year); English with a few Hinglish phrases; 350-550 words with a weekly plan; one link allowed at the end to the mentor's free study-plan PDF with affiliation stated; goal: the asker gets a usable plan and the answer earns upvotes.

verified.note: Credential line from the persona notes, direct answer in the first lines, a week-by-week plan whose hours add up (2.5 h weekdays, 6 h Sunday = 18.5 h), error-notebook and mock-analysis advice that reads first-hand, caveats (weak maths, rotating shifts, check the latest SSC notification), one link with affiliation stated, no hard sell. Brief asked for 'a few Hinglish phrases' and there is only one; the mock-phase Sunday (1 h mock + 4 h analysis) does not use the stated 6 hours.

cards.name: Radio / audio ad script
cards.summary: A timed script for a radio, FM or streaming-audio spot where voice, sound and repetition carry the brand. Good audio scripts are written for the ear: one idea, a situation the listener can picture, the brand said early and again at the end, and a phone number, name or search term said slowly enough to remember. Bad ones are print ads read aloud with a URL nobody can catch.
use_for: 10, 20, 30 and 60-second FM spots for local retail, real estate, education, healthcare and events
RJ mentions and live-read scripts
Streaming-audio ads (music apps, podcasts networks) with a companion banner
Direct-response radio with a phone number or WhatsApp number
Bilingual spots for Indian FM (Hindi-English, regional-English)
avoid: Sung brand music: genre:jingle_lyrics (the spot may carry the jingle as its sign-off)
Host-read sponsor segments in a podcast: genre:podcast_ad_read
Television or video spots: genre:tvc_script or genre:video_ad_script
Phone menus and hold messages: genre:ivr_on_hold_script
Non-commercial awareness messages: genre:public_service_announcement
