cards.goal: A listener who half-hears the spot while driving or cooking remembers the brand, the one offer and how to reach it, and acts later.

structure.does: Client, spot length, language, voices (VO, characters), music and SFX notes, pronunciation of brand and place names.
A sound, a line of dialogue or a situation that belongs to the listener's day; set the scene in seconds.
One situation or one problem the brand solves; brand name said early (within the first third).
The single offer or reason to act, said once, clearly, with one specific (price, date, distance).
Number, WhatsApp, store location with landmark, or a search term, said slowly and repeated; spell tricky names.
Brand name again plus tagline or jingle tag; any mandatory line read clearly.

length.note: Spoken words, timed aloud with music and SFX in place. Working budget: a 10-second mention about 20-25 words, a 30-second spot about 60-80, a 60-second spot about 130-160. Hindi and fast regional reads differ; always time it with the voice artist's pace.

checklist: Is the script timed aloud to the spot length with music and SFX in place?
Is the brand said within the first third and again at the end?
Is there exactly one offer or idea?
Is the response (number, WhatsApp, location, search term) said slowly and repeated, with no long URL?
Are sentences short enough to say in one breath?
Are SFX and music cues written in brackets, separate from the spoken lines?
Are brand and place pronunciations noted for the voice artist?
Does it work with no visuals (no 'see below', no 'click')?
Are offer conditions and mandatory lines included and audible?
pitfalls: Print copy read aloud (long sentences, three offers, a website path): the ear keeps one thing. Cut to one offer and one response.
Long URLs or 10-digit numbers said once: unrememberable. Use a short name to search, a memorable number said twice, or 'WhatsApp us on' with the number grouped (98xx-xx-xxxx).
Brand said only at the end: half the audience tuned in late. Say it early and close on it.
Dialogue that sounds like an ad ('Darling, have you heard about the amazing offer at...'): write how people talk, then let the announcer carry the offer.
No sound design notes: the producer guesses. Write the cues ([SFX: pressure-cooker whistle]) where they happen.
Disclaimers rushed at double speed: unclear disclosure can make the ad misleading. Keep the mandatory line short and audible.
cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second two-voice FM spot (husband-wife scene plus announcer) for a Lucknow mithai shop chain (Chaurasia Mishthan Bhandar, fictional): order Diwali gift boxes on WhatsApp, free home delivery in Lucknow on orders above Rs 999, boxes from Rs 499; audience: Lucknow families and office admins buying gifts; Hinglish written in Devanagari for the voice artists, with SFX and music cues; 60-80 spoken words; goal: listeners remember the shop name and the WhatsApp number.

verified.note: Header with voices, music and pronunciations; kitchen sound and a gift-list question set the scene in seconds; brand said by the wife inside the first third and again at the end; offer said once with both amounts spelled for the announcer; WhatsApp number in two groups, repeated; nothing visual; about 73 spoken words. The scene resolves in three lines with no small turn or laugh, so it is clear rather than memorable.

cards.name: Daily rashifal / horoscope copy
cards.summary: Daily, weekly or yearly predictions for each of the twelve rashis (zodiac signs) for newspapers, apps, websites and social posts. Good rashifal follows the publication's astrologer or chart notes, gives each sign a distinct, situation-specific reading in the same fixed structure, and stays warm and practical; bad rashifal is twelve near-identical paragraphs, fear ('accident likely'), or instructions about money and health that could hurt someone who follows them.
use_for: Daily rashifal columns for Hindi and regional dailies and news apps
Weekly, monthly and yearly forecasts (Navratri, new year, Hindu new year editions)
Astrology app daily cards and push copy
Short-video and WhatsApp channel scripts per rashi
Festival-specific rashi guidance (what to wear or offer on a festival day) supplied by an astrologer
avoid: Writing predictions with no astrologer or chart notes and presenting them as an astrologer's reading: either work from the astrologer's notes or label the column as general guidance
Aarti, katha and festival devotion: genre:devotional_content or genre:katha_narration
Personal paid consultations: those are the astrologer's own advice, not publishable copy
Selling gemstones or paid pujas inside the forecast: keep commerce out of the reading; any promotion goes in a labelled ad
buyers: Hindi and regional newspapers and news portals
Astrologers who publish under their own name
cards.value_why: Published daily by Hindi dailies and many astrology apps, which makes it a steady staff or retainer job (harvest note; no market source was fetched, so treat the value as an estimate).
cards.goal: A reader finds their sign, reads a reading that feels specific to their day, and comes back tomorrow, without being frightened or pushed into a harmful decision.

structure.does: Day, date and any panchang details the publication runs (tithi, nakshatra, rahu kaal) taken from the astrologer or panchang source, never guessed.
Rashi name in the publication's style (मेष / Aries), in the fixed order Mesh to Meen.
One sentence on the day's tone for this sign, tied to the astrologer's note.
A specific everyday situation (a pending approval, a client call, a document) with practical framing.
General tendency only (delays, expenses, good day to plan); never a buy/sell or loan instruction.
A relationship situation with a gentle suggestion.
Gentle, common-sense wellbeing note (rest, water, routine); never a diagnosis or medicine advice.

structure.part: Upay and lucky details (if the publication runs them)
structure.does: A simple, free, harmless remedy and the lucky colour/number from the astrologer's table.

length.note: Per sign 40-80 words for daily columns (480-960 for all twelve); app cards 20-35 words per sign; weekly and yearly editions run longer per sign. Space in print decides the per-sign budget.

checklist: Are all twelve signs present, in the fixed order, with the same sub-structure each?
Does each sign's reading differ in situation, not just in shuffled words?
Is it free of fear predictions (accident, death, serious illness, divorce certain)?
Is it free of specific financial instructions (buy/sell shares, take a loan) and medical instructions (stop or start medicine)?
Are remedies simple and free or low-cost, with no product or paid puja pushed?
Do panchang details and lucky numbers come from the astrologer or source table supplied?
Does it avoid repeating yesterday's lines for the same sign?
Is the language plain everyday Hindi (or the publication's language) with consistent sign names?
pitfalls: Twelve copies of one paragraph with words swapped: readers compare signs at the breakfast table. Give each sign its own situation (paperwork, travel, a sibling, a client).
Fear lines ('Durghatna ka yog hai', 'health may worsen seriously'): they frighten vulnerable readers and add nothing. Say 'drive carefully today; leave early' instead.
Money and health instructions ('Invest in shares today', 'stop your medicine'): someone will follow it. Keep to tendencies and suggest consulting a professional for decisions.
Remedies that cost money or sell something (gemstones, paid pujas): conflict of interest. Use simple free upay supplied by the astrologer.
Invented panchang or lucky numbers: take them from the astrologer's table; if missing, leave them out and flag it.
Vague filler ('Today will be good, but be careful'): give a concrete everyday cue ('a delayed payment may come through after noon').
cards.exemplar_brief: Daily rashifal for a Hindi news app for one date, all twelve rashis from मेष to मीन, built from the astrologer's supplied one-line notes per sign and lucky colour/number table below; each sign 45-60 words covering mood, career, money tendency, family and a gentle health line, plus a free upay where the notes give one; Hindi (Devanagari); 600-750 words in all; framed as astrological guidance, no fear, money or medical instructions; goal: readers check their sign and return tomorrow. Astrologer's notes (demo data for this test): मंगलवार, 20 अक्टूबर 2026, आश्विन शुक्ल दशमी (विजयादशमी). मेष: रुका भुगतान दोपहर बाद मिलने के आसार; भाई-बहन से बात नरमी से; लाल, 9; उपाय: हनुमान चालीसा का पाठ। वृषभ: काग़ज़ात दोबारा जाँचें; शाम को परिवार के साथ बाहर जाना; सफ़ेद, 6। मिथुन: यात्रा की योजना बनेगी, देर से न निकलें; क्लाइंट की पूरी बात सुनें; हरा, 5। कर्क: घर की पुरानी योजना माँ से बात करके आगे बढ़ेगी; क्रीम, 2; उपाय: शिवलिंग पर जल। सिंह: दफ़्तर में आपकी बात का वज़न रहेगा, अहंकार से बचें; सुनहरा, 1। कन्या: हिसाब-किताब की छोटी गलती पकड़ में आएगी; खाना हल्का रखें; गहरा हरा, 7। तुला: दोस्त की सलाह काम आएगी; गुलाबी, 4। वृश्चिक: पुराने सहकर्मी से मतभेद सुलझेगा; शाम को थकान, जल्दी सोएँ; मरून, 3। धनु: पढ़ाई या प्रशिक्षण में अच्छी ख़बर; बच्चों को समय दें; पीला, 3; उपाय: तुलसी को जल। मकर: काम का बोझ बढ़ेगा पर टीम साथ देगी; पिता से सलाह लें; नीला, 8। कुंभ: नए संपर्क से काम की बात बनेगी; सोशल मीडिया पर संयम; आसमानी, 4। मीन: रचनात्मक काम में मन लगेगा; देर रात तक न जागें; केसरिया, 7; उपाय: गाय को रोटी।

verified.note: All twelve rashis in order with the same mood/career/money/family/health/upay pattern, each with its own everyday situation, free harmless upay, no fear, money or medicine instructions, an advisory line at the top, panchang and lucky table left as placeholders rather than guessed. Natural Hindi. The money line falls into one template ('dhan ke maamle mein aaj...') in five signs. The readings are the writer's general drafts, not the astrologer's notes, because the card supplied none. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> include the twelve one-line astrologer notes and the lucky colour/number table (and the date with tithi), or drop 'supplied' and say the readings are general. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_c): exemplar_brief now includes the twelve astrologer one-line notes, the lucky colour/number table, free upay and the date with tithi; re-judge pending.

cards.name: README (project front page)
cards.summary: The first file a visitor reads in a code repository: what the project is, why it is useful, how to install it and run a first example, where to get help and how to contribute. Good READMEs let a stranger go from landing to a working first run in minutes with copy-pasteable commands; bad ones open with badges and history and bury the install step.
use_for: Open-source libraries, CLIs and tools
Internal repositories that other teams must set up and run
Developer-tool launches where the README is the landing page
Templates, starter kits and sample apps
Data, model and dataset repositories (with usage and licence terms)
avoid: Full endpoint-by-endpoint documentation: genre:api_reference (link it from the README)
A step-by-step learning walkthrough: genre:developer_tutorial
End-user help for a finished product: genre:user_manual or genre:knowledge_base_article
Version-by-version change lists: genre:release_notes or a CHANGELOG file

sources.title: GitHub Docs: About READMEs
sources.supports: A README typically covers what the project does, why it is useful, how users get started, where users can get help, and who maintains and contributes; GitHub shows the first README found in .github, then the repository root, then docs; content beyond 500 KiB is truncated; GitHub auto-generates an outline from headings; relative links are recommended over absolute ones

sources.title: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: Technical Writers
sources.supports: 'The median annual wage for technical writers was $90,390 in May 2025'; employment projected to grow 1 percent from 2025 to 2035

sources.title: AmbitionBox: Technical Writer salary in India
sources.supports: 'The average salary for a Technical Writer is Rs 8.5 Lakhs per year' (10.1k salaries, updated 4 Oct 2026)

cards.value_why: Usually written in-house by developers; paid when bundled with open-source launches, developer-tool marketing or documentation projects. It sits inside technical writing, which pays well: BLS median $90,390 (May 2025) and AmbitionBox India average Rs 8.5 L a year (Oct 2026).
cards.goal: A developer who has never seen the project installs it and runs a working first example, then knows where to look next.

structure.does: What it is and for whom, in plain words ('A CLI that validates GSTINs in a CSV, offline').
Only the few that answer real questions (build status, version, licence).
The problem it solves and 3-6 things it does; a screenshot or GIF with alt text if visual.
Prerequisites with versions, the install command, and the smallest example that works when pasted, with its expected output.
Common tasks, each with a short heading, a code block and one line on the result.
Options, flags or environment variables in a table: name, default, what it does.
Links to full docs, issues, discussions or chat; what to include in a bug report.
How to set up for development and run tests, or a link to CONTRIBUTING.md.
Licence name with link; maintainers and acknowledgements.

length.note: Small utilities need 150-400 words; frameworks and platforms keep the README to quick start and links (under about 1,500 words) and move depth into docs. GitHub truncates READMEs beyond 500 KiB.

checklist: Does the first line say what the project does and for whom?
Is there an install command and a minimal example that runs as pasted?
Are prerequisites listed with versions?
Does the quick start show the expected output so the reader knows it worked?
Are commands in fenced code blocks with the language marked?
Does it say where to get help and how to report bugs?
Is the licence named and linked?
Are links relative for files inside the repo?
Is it free of 'simply', 'just' and 'obviously' around steps that may not be simple?
pitfalls: History and philosophy before install: move them below usage; the first screen is name, purpose, quick start.
Examples that do not run (missing import, old flag): test every command on a clean machine before publishing.
Assuming the reader's setup ('just run make'): list prerequisites and OS differences (Windows paths, Python version).
Wall of badges: keep the few that answer questions; badges are not documentation.
Screenshots with no alt text and text inside images: add alt text and keep commands as copyable text.
No licence: others cannot legally reuse the code. Name the licence and add the LICENSE file.

require.label: has an install or run command

cards.exemplar_brief: README for an open-source Python CLI by a Bengaluru developer (gstcheck, fictional) that validates the format and check digit of GSTINs in a vendor CSV, offline, and writes a report of invalid rows; install via pip, Python 3.10+, MIT licence; include quick start with sample CSV and expected output, three usage examples, a flags table, help and contributing sections; English; 400-700 words; goal: an accounts-team developer installs it and checks their vendor CSV within 5 minutes.

verified.note: First line says what it does; why section names the real pain (ITC mismatch) and what it does not do (no registration check); Python 3.10+ prerequisite, pip install, a pasteable sample CSV and exact expected output; three usage examples, flags table, help with what to put in a bug report, contributing commands, MIT with a relative LICENSE link. Check digits verified: 08ABCDE1234F1Z0 and 29PQRSX5678L1ZS are valid, 27AAAPL1234C1Z expects E, line numbers match the file. lint_suspect upheld: the two '!' are Markdown image syntax for badges. CARD FIX: lint.max_exclamations -> drop it for genre:readme (or have pcw.py ignore '![' before counting). | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_c): lint.max_exclamations dropped (badge image syntax '![' was being counted); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Real estate listing / project copy
cards.summary: Property descriptions for resale and rental listings, and project copy for brochures, ads and microsites, written to get the right buyers or tenants to enquire. Good listing copy leads with configuration, carpet area, locality and the one standout fact, then describes the home from what a visitor will actually see; bad copy is 'luxurious dream home in a prime location' with no area, floor or distance.
use_for: Resale and rental listings on property portals and broker websites
WhatsApp and Instagram versions of a listing for broker groups
New-project brochure copy, site banners and ad copy
Project microsite sections (location, amenities, floor plans)
Commercial space, plot and holiday-home listings
avoid: Hotel, homestay and Airbnb listings: genre:hospitality_listing
Full brochure design narratives for any business: genre:brochure_copy
Newspaper project ads: genre:print_ad_copy, keeping this card's facts and disclosures
Describing amenities, approvals or distances you have not confirmed: get them from the client in writing first

sources.title: Fiverr: Product Descriptions subcategory
sources.supports: page search data on 2026-10-04: num_found 4945 gigs; platform filter includes Property listings/Real estate

sources.title: Wikipedia: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016
sources.supports: Registration is mandatory for launching a project; builders must quote prices based on carpet area, not super built-up area; carpet area is defined in section 2(k) and includes usable spaces like kitchen and toilets

buyers: NRI owners selling or renting through agents
cards.value_why: Fiverr's Product Descriptions subcategory lists Property listings/Real estate as its own platform filter (4,945 gigs in the subcategory, Oct 2026). Developers buy project copy through agencies; brokers buy listing copy in volume.
cards.goal: A qualified buyer or tenant (right budget, right needs) books a site visit or calls, and unqualified ones self-select out.

structure.does: Configuration + carpet area + locality + the standout fact ('2 BHK, 820 sq ft carpet, Wakad: 1.5 km to Hinjewadi Phase 1').

Price (and whether negotiable), carpet area, floor of total floors, facing, age or possession date, parking, maintenance, furnishing; for projects, RERA registration number and the disclosure line the client's legal team requires.
Who the home suits and the main reason to see it, in plain words.
Rooms, light and ventilation, views, fittings, storage, recent work; only what a visitor will see.
Lifts, power backup, security, water, clubhouse: only what exists and works today.
Named places with real distances or drive times (school, metro, IT park, hospital, market).
Brokerage, documents ready, loan-approved banks if true, visit timings, phone/WhatsApp.

length.note: Portal resale and rental listings: 120-250 words plus the facts block. WhatsApp versions: 50-90 words. Project brochure sections run longer, but each section follows the same facts-first rule.

checklist: Does the headline give configuration, carpet area and locality?
Is the area stated as carpet area (with super built-up, if given at all, clearly labelled)?
Are price, floor, facing, age or possession and parking stated?
Is every amenity and distance confirmed by the client and specific (named place, km or minutes)?
For a new project: is the RERA registration number and the required disclosure line present or flagged?
Is it free of vague hype (prime location, dream home, world-class amenities)?
Are AI renders or virtual staging labelled as such?
Is there a clear CTA with visit timings and contact?
pitfalls: Hype instead of facts ('luxurious living in a prime location'): buyers filter by facts. Lead with BHK, carpet sq ft, floor, facing and price.
Super built-up area passed off as size: misleads buyers and, for registered projects, prices must be quoted on carpet area. Say 'carpet area' explicitly.
Distances as wishes ('minutes from the airport'): give the named place and real km or peak-hour minutes.
Amenities that are 'proposed' described as existing: misleading-ad rules apply. Mark them as under construction with the expected date from the developer.
Rendered images or AI-staged rooms presented as real: label them; ASCI's 2026 synthetic-content guidelines expect it.
Project ad without the registration details: ask the client's legal team for the RERA number and required line before anything goes live.

ban.label: vague property hype
ban.regex: (?i)\b(luxurious living|dream home|world[- ]class amenities|prime location|heaven on earth|once in a lifetime)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Resale listing for a property portal plus a WhatsApp version for broker groups: 2 BHK in Wakad, Pune, 820 sq ft carpet, 7th floor of 12, east-facing, 6 years old, one covered car park, society with gym and 24-hour security, Rs 78 lakh negotiable (about Rs 9,500 per sq ft carpet), 1.5 km to Hinjewadi Phase 1 gate, 10 minutes to Greenfield CBSE School (name invented for this demo); English for the portal (150-250 words with a facts block), Hinglish allowed for the 50-80-word WhatsApp version; goal: IT professionals with a matching budget book a weekend visit. Owner's interior facts (demo data for this test): 2 bathrooms, one attached to the master bedroom; one balcony off the living room, east-facing; vitrified tile flooring; semi-furnished with a modular kitchen with chimney and 3 wardrobes; maintenance Rs 3,200 a month; vacant, ready to move.

verified.note: Headline has configuration, carpet area, locality and the standout distance; facts block complete with gaps flagged; opening says who it suits (Hinjewadi Phase 1 commuters); location bullets use only the supplied distances; WhatsApp version is tight Hinglish with one bold line. Weak spots: the opening and 'The home' restate the facts block (the car park appears three times) and 'The home' is mostly a placeholder. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> name the CBSE school it says is 'named', and add two or three interior facts (bathrooms, balcony, flooring, furnishing, maintenance) so the 150-250 words can describe the home instead of repeating the facts. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_c): exemplar_brief now names the CBSE school and adds interior facts (bathrooms, balcony, flooring, furnishing, maintenance, per-sq-ft price); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Recipe post
cards.summary: A food-blog article with a short intro, ingredient list, numbered method, timings, yield and tips, formatted so a reader can cook from it on a phone with messy hands. Good recipe posts put the recipe within one scroll (or a jump link), give quantities and visual cues ('until oil separates, 6-8 minutes'), and answer the substitutions people ask about; bad ones bury the recipe under 1,500 words of memories.
use_for: Food blogs and recipe sites
Brand recipe content for spice, oil, appliance and FMCG companies
Regional and festival recipe series (Chhath thekua, Onam sadya, Bihari litti chokha)
Companion articles for recipe reels and YouTube videos
Cookbook-style recipe pages for D2C food brands
avoid: Non-food step-by-step guides: genre:how_to_article
A recipe reel or short: genre:short_form_video_script (link the post from it)
Restaurant menus: genre:restaurant_menu_copy
Health or diet claims about a dish (cures, fat-burning): describe ingredients and nutrition only from a qualified source

sources.title: Fiverr: Articles & Blog Posts category (facets read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Article type filter (Instructional/How-to 3138 gigs); harvest notes the Topic facet lists Food & beverage at 263 gigs

sources.title: Google Search Central: Recipe structured data
sources.supports: Google's documentation for marking up recipes with schema.org Recipe structured data (a separate SEO task from the writing)

buyers: Spice, oil, flour and appliance brands
Cloud kitchens and D2C food brands
Cooking-creator teams turning videos into posts
cards.value_why: Fiverr's article Topic facet lists Food & beverage at 263 gigs (Oct 2026), a mid-sized niche; most food bloggers write their own. Paid work comes mainly from food and appliance brands and from creators who need posts from their videos.
cards.goal: A reader cooks the dish successfully the first time, from their phone, without leaving the page to look something up.

structure.does: Dish + the trait people search for (method, time, region, diet): 'Bihari litti chokha in the oven (no tandoor, 50 minutes)'.
A 'Jump to recipe' link and one line on what makes this version work.
Why this version, where the dish comes from, what the reader needs to know before starting (soaking, special pan). Personal story only if it helps the cook.
Prep time, cook time, total time, servings or yield, difficulty, equipment.
Grouped by component (dough, filling, chokha); exact quantities with units (g, cups, tsp) and prep state ('1 onion, finely chopped'); local names with alternates.
Numbered steps, one action each, with heat level, time and a visual or sensory cue for doneness.
What to swap, what goes wrong and how to fix it (dough cracking, filling too dry).
How long it keeps, how to reheat, what to serve with.
2-4 questions readers actually ask (can I air-fry it, make it ahead, skip the ghee).
The printable card with the same data, marked up with Recipe structured data by the site's plugin.

length.note: Simple recipes run 400-800 words; multi-component regional dishes with technique notes run 1,000-1,500. Length should come from cues, tips and fixes, not preamble.

checklist: Can the reader reach the ingredients within one scroll or via a jump link?
Are prep, cook and total times and the yield stated?
Does every ingredient have a quantity and unit (or 'to taste' only for salt and similar)?
Is each method step one action with a time or a doneness cue?
Are local ingredient names given with an alternative for readers elsewhere?
Does it cover at least two substitutions or fixes for common problems?
Are storage and reheating covered?
If a brand's product is featured for payment, is that disclosed?
pitfalls: Life story before the recipe: readers hate the scroll. Keep the intro short and add the jump link at the top.
'Cook till done' and 'a little masala': beginners fail. Give the time range and the cue ('till the raw smell goes and oil separates, 6-8 minutes').
Cups for some ingredients, grams for others, 'katori' for the rest: pick one system with conversions for flour and rice.
Untested recipe rewritten from another site: quantities are often wrong and it is plagiarism. Cook it, or work from the client's tested recipe.
Health halo claims ('this dal cures acidity', 'fat-burning'): unsupported. Describe what is in it, not what it cures.
Brand-sponsored post without disclosure: ASCI's influencer guidelines apply to sponsored recipe content. Add the disclosure at the top.
cards.exemplar_brief: Recipe post for a Patna home-cook blog: Bihari litti chokha made in a home oven (no tandoor or coal), 12 littis with sattu filling plus baingan-aloo-tamatar chokha; audience: Bihari families living in metros and first-time cooks; English with Hindi dish and ingredient names; 900-1,300 words with jump link, at-a-glance block, grouped ingredients, numbered steps with doneness cues, air-fryer variation, three fixes and a short FAQ; goal: a reader cooks it successfully the first time.

verified.note: Recipe within one scroll after a short useful intro, at-a-glance block, grouped ingredients with grams and local names, ten numbered steps with heat, time and doneness cues (damp-sand filling, hollow tap), quantities reconcile (about 600 g dough for 12 x 50 g), air-fryer variation, three fixes plus two substitutions, storage and reheating, FAQ. Writer notes it was not test-cooked; quantities and times look standard. The intro promises 'the same smoky chokha' from oven heat alone, which oven-roasted baingan will not fully deliver; suggest a gas-flame char as optional.

cards.name: Letter of recommendation (LOR)
cards.summary: A letter from a teacher, professor or manager vouching for a candidate with specific evidence: how long and in what role they know the candidate, how the candidate compares with peers, and two or three concrete episodes that show the qualities the programme or employer is looking for. It must be in the recommender's voice and signed and submitted by them. Good LORs read like one person who knows the candidate well; bad ones are 'hard-working and sincere' templates any student could get.
use_for: Graduate admissions (MS, MBA, PhD) in India and abroad
Undergraduate admissions abroad (teacher and counsellor letters)
Scholarships, fellowships and exchange programmes
Job references and visa or immigration support letters from employers
Drafts prepared for a busy professor or manager to edit and sign
avoid: The applicant's own story and goals: genre:statement_of_purpose or genre:college_essay
A standard employment or experience certificate (dates, designation): use the HR template, not a persuasive letter
Drafting for a recommender who has not agreed to review, edit and submit it: many programmes want the recommender to write and submit directly; check the rules and do not ghost-submit
Praise the recommender cannot back with examples: a shorter, specific letter beats a long generic one

sources.title: SOP Expert (India)
sources.supports: Indian agency selling SOP, LOR and admission-essay writing for study abroad

buyers: Study-abroad applicants and their counselling agencies
Professors and managers who ask for a first draft
cards.value_why: Indian study-abroad agencies (e.g. SOP Expert) sell LOR drafting alongside SOPs; applicants usually need two or three letters per application cycle, so it comes bundled with SOP work.
cards.goal: The admissions committee or employer believes, from specific evidence, that this candidate stands out among peers in the qualities the programme values.

structure.does: Institution or company letterhead, date, 'To the Admissions Committee, <programme, university>' where known.
Who the recommender is, how long and in what capacity they have known the candidate, and the overall strength of the recommendation.
How the candidate ranks among peers the recommender has taught or managed, with the basis (course, cohort size, year), only if true.
Two or three specific episodes: the situation, what the candidate did, the result, and what it shows (research ability, leadership, persistence). Map them to the programme's criteria.
An honest note on growth or an area still developing, framed with evidence of improvement.
A clear recommendation tied to the programme, and an offer to answer questions.
Name, designation, department, institution, official email and phone.

length.note: One page (300-500 words) is common for Indian undergraduate and job references; graduate admissions letters with research detail run 500-800. Some portals impose limits or ask rating questions instead; follow them.

checklist: Does the opening say how long and in what capacity the recommender knows the candidate?
Is there at least one comparison with peers, with its basis, that the recommender confirms is true?
Are there two or three specific episodes with what the candidate did and what resulted?
Do the episodes match what this programme or role looks for?
Is it written in the recommender's voice, with details only they would know?
Is it free of generic praise words without evidence (hard-working, sincere, punctual)?
Does it differ in substance from the candidate's other letters and SOP (no copied phrases)?
Does it close with a signature block with official contact details?
Has the recommender reviewed, edited and agreed to submit it themselves?
pitfalls: Template praise ('She is a hard-working and sincere student'): committees discount it. Replace with an episode: 'She rebuilt our battery test rig in two weekends when the lab's logger failed.'
Three letters from the same pen: same phrases and structure across recommenders look ghost-written. Draft each from that recommender's own notes and let their voice show.
Invented rankings ('top 1% of students I have ever taught'): the recommender must confirm every claim; use the real basis ('3rd of 68 in Heat Transfer, 2024').
Applicant-drafted letter submitted without the recommender's real review: can breach an application's honesty rules. The recommender edits, owns and submits it.
Repeating the CV (marks, courses): the committee has the transcript. Add what the transcript cannot show.
No link to the programme: name what the candidate will bring to this kind of programme (research, team projects, industry work).

ban.label: template praise
ban.regex: (?i)\b(hard[- ]?working and sincere|sincere and hard[- ]?working|punctual and obedient|any (university|organi[sz]ation) would be lucky)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: LOR from a Pune engineering-college professor (fictional) for a mechanical-engineering student applying to MS programmes in Germany and the US: recommender's notes supplied (taught her Heat Transfer and Thermal Systems Design, ranked 3rd of 68 in Heat Transfer in 2024, guided her final-year project on battery thermal management for electric two-wheelers, she rebuilt the lab's test rig and co-wrote a conference paper); English; 450-600 words on letterhead; drafted for the professor to edit, sign and submit himself; goal: the admissions committee sees specific evidence of research ability and initiative.

verified.note: Opening states role, length and courses; uses the supplied rank (3rd of 68, 2024) as the comparison; frames the rig rebuild and the co-written paper as evidence of research ability and initiative, with good reasoning on why rig work matters; signature block. Many episode details are placeholders (the notes were thin). Craft slip: the close names both Germany and the United States ('I expect her to hold her own in either country'); a letter goes to one programme, so name that programme and drop the other country. 'Evidence rather than adjectives' is a slight writerly tell.
